newsitem.title: UK: Focus - Precious metals soar, oil sags in February.
newsitem.headline: Focus - Precious metals soar, oil sags in February.

text.p: Speculators took profits and put the brakes on a dramatic rally in precious metals prices on Friday, but the market has ended the month with prospects of new gains on fears that labour unrest might disrupt supply from Russia of platinum and palladium.

Palladium prices were up 25 percent and those for its sister rare white metal platinum by 17 percent at the end of February compared with a month ago. Gold and copper were among other items to gain in value in the commodity sector during February.
Crude oil was the big loser - down almost $5 to around $19 per barrel for the bellwether North Sea Brent Blend.
Friday saw platinum reach $406 per ounce before speculators took profits. It closed in London at $389.90.
Dealers said concerns over the non-appearance of Russian exports of the precious metal so far this year were fuelling demand especially in Japan, the largest consumer of platinum.
And unions have now threatened a possible strike at Russia's Arctic Norilsk mining and metallurgical complex from March 15. The last time workers were paid in full was for October 1996.
Platinum's sister metal palladium fixed at $157.00 on Thursday, its highest fixing since July 1995, although it also eased to end Friday at $151.50.
Gold ended in London at $358.45 which is a gain of seven percent from a 3-3/4 year low hit in mid-February just above $336. Gold is being helped up by the white metals, dealers say.

Russia is the biggest producer of palladium and the second largest after South Africa of platinum, mainly used in electronics and auto catalysts to clean up exhaust fumes. Japan is by far the largest consumer.
The industrial base metals were little changed on Friday.
Copper is ending February just below $2,400 per tonne and is up more than 10 percent since the beginning of the month on tight nearby supply.
Aluminium has not been quite such a brisk performer. It ended Friday afternoon on the London Metal Exchange at $1,654 per tonne, compared with $1,610 at the end of January.
Lead firmed in a technical market to touch $705 per tonne before easing again, a gain of $23.
World oil prices staggered lower again on a view that rising supplies would continue to outweigh demand in the gap between the winter heating oil and summer gasoline seasons.
Bellwether North Sea Brent fell to around $19.20 per barrel, extending a 20 percent slide from just below $25 in January.

"I think the market's got the potential to go a lot lower," said Nauman Barakat at brokers Prudential Bache. "Sentiment is still bearish on heating oil and crude and there's no concern yet about tightness in gasoline."
Rising Iraqi exports under the United Nations oil-for-food exchange remained at the centre of market concerns.
Coffee has remained volatile through February. Despite hitting new cyclical highs on concerns about Latin American supply, the London nearby Robusta contract hasn't risen very far since a month ago.
It was trading just under $1,600 per tonne in London on Friday after a February peak at $1,705 and compared with around $1,530 at the end of January.

Other commodities were not much changed on the day, although Chicago wheat futures eased on news that Australia clinched a big sale to Japan. Wheat, cocoa and sugar were also little changed from the start of February.
